會說話的鼓屬膜鳴樂器，常見於西非格里奧音樂、約魯巴與達貢巴的格里奧傳統，以及塞雷: The talking drum is a membranophone, common in West African griot music, in the griot traditions of the Yoruba and the Dagomba, and in the drum set of the Serer tama in the Uwong / Haat ceremony. It also appears in twentieth-century West African popular music, such as mbalax in Senegal and fuji and juju in Nigeria; it is used at weddings, funerals and private occasions, and in the line-up of African bands.
會說話的鼓採用沙漏形木製鼓身，通常由非洲硬木（如紅木）製成。鼓的上下兩端各裝有動: The talking drum has an hourglass-shaped wooden body, usually of an African hardwood such as mahogany. Animal-hide heads are fitted at both ends, usually of goatskin or cowhide. The heads are joined by leather tension cords, and the player changes the pitch by adjusting their tension. The cords are of leather or plant fibre, which keeps them durable and flexible. The internal resonating chamber strengthens the resonance, so the whole structure serves both traditional craft and acoustics.

The talking drum is a West African hourglass-shaped double-headed membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.242.11. It has two heads joined by leather tension cords; the player tucks the drum under the arm and squeezes the cords with the arm and body, changing the tension of the heads and the pitch, imitating the tones and rhythms of human speech. Griots and drummers of peoples such as the Yoruba, Ashanti and Serer use it in ceremonies, weddings, funerals, the calling of warriors or the sending of messages, and it is also used in mbalax, fuji and juju music and in African bands.
會說話的鼓音色溫潤而富有表現力，兼具低沉與尖銳的雙重特質。其音域寬廣，可從深沉的: The talking drum has a warm, expressive timbre, both deep and sharp. Its range is wide, from a deep bass up to a clear high, and the player changes pitch smoothly by tightening or loosening the tension cords. The vibration of the head gives a distinctive resonance, soft in quality yet strong, with a clearly voice-like character. Unlike an ordinary drum, whose sound is dry, the talking drum is more like singing, as if speech were rising and falling. Its sound sits between percussion and a national instrument: it has the weight of a drum and also something of the glissando of a string instrument, so that it can imitate human speech and feeling.
會說話的鼓（211.242.11）為西非沙漏形雙面膜鳴鼓，以皮繩連接兩鼓面，夾於: The talking drum (211.242.11) is a West African hourglass-shaped double-headed membranophone whose two heads are joined by a leather cord and tuned by squeezing the drum under the arm. Its history can be traced to peoples including the Bono, the Yoruba, the Ghana Empire and the Hausa, and it is the core of griot music. From the eighteenth century drummers passed ritual messages and commands by pitch, and Europeans noticed this use in the first half of the eighteenth century. Variants that are not hourglass-shaped later appeared, such as the dùndún and the fontomfrom, and the drum is limited to West Africa, with exceptions in northern Cameroon and western Chad. In the twentieth century it entered popular music such as mbalax, fuji and juju, and is also used at weddings and funerals and in band line-ups.
演奏者將沙漏形鼓身夾於腋下與肋骨之間，以手臂壓迫或放鬆皮繩，改變兩面鼓皮的張力，: The player tucks the hourglass body between arm and ribs, pressing or releasing the leather cords with the arm to change the tension of the two heads and so raise or lower the note; a slide can also be squeezed out within one beat. A beginner should practise holding the drum steady and controlling the tension with the arm, then strike short phrases and pauses following the rise and fall of speech. To send messages, each word must be remembered as a fixed phrase, which supplies context and reduces ambiguity.
